newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: Conservative economics to dominate S.Africa budget.
newsitem.headline: Conservative economics to dominate S.Africa budget.

text.p: South Africa's ANC-led government is likely to please financial markets but dismay its allies on the left with its 1997/98 budget next week, analysts said on Wednesday.

Trevor Manuel, the country's first African National Congress (ANC) finance minister, will present a budget on March 12 of real spending cuts designed to slice into the country's debt mountain and sell South Africa to global investors, they said.
His maiden budget comes half-way through the government's first term in office and is arguably the most important yet of the post-apartheid era.
Markets are looking for confirmation of its commitment to market-oriented reform, first laid out in the Growth, Employment and Redistribution (GEAR) strategy last June.

There is also widespread speculation that Manuel will announce the next cautious steps in the gradual removal of foreign exchange controls in, or ahead of, the budget, focusing this time on the needs of individuals wishing to invest abroad.
The key budget number is already known. Manuel has pledged a deficit before borrowing of four percent of gross domestic product (GDP), without including privatisation receipts.
This represents a reduction from 5.1 percent in the current year and 8.5 percent in 1992/93, leaving little room for manoeuvre.
Economists say the figure is achievable by keeping a tight rein on expenditure and further improving tax collection.

They predict spending will rise close to eight percent -- less than current inflation of 9.4 percent -- to just under 190 billion rand ($42 billion) while revenue is seen going up some 12 percent at close to 165 billion.
The details will be closely watched, according to SMK Securities economist Herman van Papendorp who said the markets wanted to see more capital expenditure and less recurrent.

"We know the deficit before borrowing will be four percent but just how he is going to achieve it is still a very important question," said Ben van Rensburg, director of economic policy at the South African Chamber of Business.

With a deficit of around 25 billion rand and government bond redemptions of around 10.5 billion, South Africa would face a borrowing requirement of around 35-36 billion in 1997/98 (April-March), against a revised 39 billion this year.

Borrowing needs could be cut further, to 30-33 billion, if the government uses some of the proceeds from the privatisation of Telkom, other state assets and the sale of strategic oil stocks to retire debt.
That may be good news for the bond market but will not satisfy trade unions who have called for higher spending on housing, health and education to cut gaping inequalities.
Labour would also like increased taxes on the rich, on business and on luxury goods -- none of which are expected.
Analysts predict no meaningful changes in value added, income or company taxes. However, "sin taxes" on alcohol and tobacco may be hiked, along with a levy on fuel.

All in all, Reserve Bank Governor Chris Stals is confident that the budget will show fiscal displicine and demonstrate that South Africa is on track its GEAR programme, designed to double growth to six percent a year by 2000.

"I am sure that it will confirm again to the market that the South African government is able and determined to implement the structural adjustments necessary to raise the growth potential of the economy to higher levels," he said this week.
